content: 1. Healthcare should be provided to individuals and communities based on their specific needs. 2. Efficient healthcare delivery involves maximizing the use of available resources while minimizing waste. 3. Accessible healthcare ensures that services are provided in a timely manner, are geographically reasonable, and are delivered in settings equipped with the appropriate skills and resources to meet medical needs. 4. Acceptable or patient-centered healthcare takes into account the preferences, aspirations, and cultural contexts of individual service users and their communities. 5. Equitable healthcare delivery ensures that the quality of care does not vary based on personal characteristics such as gender, race, ethnicity, geographical location, or socioeconomic status. 6. Safe healthcare delivery minimizes risks and harm to service users. 7. Rehabilitation consists of measures designed to help individuals who experience or are at risk of experiencing disability to achieve and maintain optimal functioning in interaction with their environments. 8. Rehabilitation services include rehabilitation medicine, therapy, and assistive technology. 9. Residential care facilities, such as nursing homes or long-term care facilities, primarily provide long-term residential care that combines nursing, supervisory, or other types of care as required by the residents. 10. These facilities offer a mix of health and social services, with health services primarily at the level of nursing care, combined with personal care services. 11. The medical components of care in residential facilities are less intensive than those provided in hospitals. 12. Respite care is often provided in older people’s homes but can also occur in day centers or residential facilities. 13. For care recipients, respite care involves participation in enjoyable, meaningful activities that promote social engagement, companionship, and stimulation. 14. Respite care supports individuals in living in the community for as long as possible and is delivered in a dignified and respectful manner. 15. For caregivers, respite care provides time away from their caregiving role to engage in other activities of their choice, with the assurance that the care recipient is receiving quality care. 16. Respite care contributes to the goal of supporting aging in place, ensuring high-quality care for individuals, including those with dementia, and reducing health risks for caregivers. 17. Responsive referral protocols and pathways clearly outline the indications for referrals and the responsibilities of each healthcare professional and department involved. 18. Restraints refer to the use of mechanical devices, physical methods, or medications to voluntarily prevent a person from moving their body. 19. Seclusion involves the voluntary placement of an individual alone in a locked room or secured area from which they are physically prevented from leaving. 20. Alternatives to seclusion include prompt assessment and rapid intervention during potential crises, as well as the use of problem-solving methods and stress management techniques such as breathing exercises. 21. Secondary care refers to specialist care provided on an outpatient or inpatient basis, typically following a referral from primary care. 22. Social and financial protection benefits include financial transfers to households to address needs arising from circumstances such as housing, education, family situations, sickness, retirement, or unemployment. 23. These benefits also encompass economic or social support provided by the government, such as paid or unpaid leave, credited social contributions, tax allowances, duty rebates, discounted transportation fares, and free companion fares, particularly for individuals with dementia and their caregivers. 24. Social care involves assistance with activities of daily living, such as personal care and maintaining the home. It is also referred to as home and community care. 25. A social worker is a professional who has completed formal training in social work at a recognized university-level institution, earning a diploma or degree in social work. 26. Social workers in relevant fields, such as geriatrics, mental health, and neurology, may provide treatment or care for individuals with dementia. 27. Social media refers to web-based technologies used for communication between organizations, communities, and individuals. Common examples include platforms like Facebook and Twitter. 28. Specialist medical doctors are professionals who diagnose, treat, and prevent illnesses, diseases, injuries, and other physical and mental impairments using specialized testing, diagnostic, medical, surgical, physical, and psychiatric techniques. 29. These specialists focus on specific disease categories, patient types, or treatment methods. 30. For the purposes of the GDO, specialist medical doctor refers to groups such as geriatricians, psychogeriatricians, old-age psychiatrists, as well as psychiatrists and neurologists who can diagnose dementia and provide treatment for individuals with dementia. 31. A stakeholder is an individual, group, or organization with an interest in the delivery and organization of healthcare. 32. A standard is an established, accepted, and evidence-based technical specification or basis for comparison. National standards provide foundational principles for care delivery and progress measurement. 33. A strategy is a long-term plan designed to achieve a specific goal. 34. Subnational refers to individual states, territories, provinces, or regions within a country. 35. Supported decision-making is a model endorsed by the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, enabling individuals with mental disabilities to nominate a trusted person or network to consult and discuss issues affecting them, including decision-making. 36. Task shifting involves delegating selected tasks to existing or new healthcare professionals with either less training or more narrowly focused training. 37. An interdisciplinary team consists of members who work interdependently to develop goals and a common treatment plan while maintaining distinct professional responsibilities and individual assignments. Leadership functions are shared in these teams. 38. A multidisciplinary team consists of members from different disciplines, sometimes from one or more organizations, working on the same task (e.g., assessing individuals, setting goals, and making care recommendations) but functioning independently. These teams are traditionally led by the highest-ranking team member. 39. Tertiary care involves the provision of highly specialized services in ambulatory and hospital settings or facilities equipped for advanced medical investigation and treatment. 40. A national dementia unit or department is a unit or department within a Ministry of Health (or equivalent) or national institute responsible for dementia-related matters. 41. Universal health coverage ensures that all individuals receive the healthcare services they need without experiencing financial hardship when paying for them. 42. Data sharing is essential for sound public health actions, with recognized benefits including scientific and public health advancements. 43. WHO promotes the sharing of health data, including surveillance and epidemiological data, while ensuring compliance with national laws, including data protection laws. 44. Data providers confirm that data shared with WHO have been collected in accordance with applicable laws and agree to WHO’s use, publication, and dissemination of the data for public health purposes, subject to ethical and secure use measures. 45. Data providers may opt out of certain data-sharing provisions by notifying WHO in writing, specifying the data in question, the scope of the opt-out, and the reasons for it.
